findings.where: The logo: the small mark and 'MMM INFRA' lockup in the nav bar, and the large mark in the hero (phone and desktop)
findings.fault: The logo has been recoloured. The arches are in the palette's near-black 'cut' rather than the logo's own grey, and the wordmark is near-black instead of the logo blue. The logo blue appears nowhere in the palette. It is not a token with a job and it is not set aside as a logo-only colour, so this direction gives the real full-colour logo no ground it can stand on.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose brief says the logo stays and is never redrawn. Visitors who know MMM Infra's blue-and-grey mark from his current site or LinkedIn would see a different company's mark.

findings.where: Palette: minium red used for the hero name, the article title, the motion-sketch words and the 'Write to Mark' button
findings.fault: The red is meant to mark the one action, but it also fills every large heading. On the first screen the red name at about 64 px outweighs the small red button below it. The colour that should send the eye to the action goes to the headline instead, which undercuts the direction's own rule of one accent that flows to the action.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank visitor scanning for how to get in touch. With red on every heading, the button no longer stands out as the one place to act.

findings.where: Article specimen: the pull quote in a tabula ansata frame, compared with the 'Write to Mark' button in the hero
findings.fault: The quote and the button share one shape: a box with dovetail triangles on both sides. The page uses one look for a static quote and for the main action. The quote is outlined in dark and the button filled in red, but the handles are the button's identifying shape, so the quote looks like a large button.
findings.who_objects: A reader of an article page, who may tap the quote expecting it to do something. They then learn that the dovetail shape does not reliably mean 'act'.

findings.where: Overall ground and tone: flat granite grey across the whole page, Roman capitals painted red, the tablet frames
findings.fault: Mid-grey stone with carved red capitals and inscription tablets reads as a monument or memorial plaque. The result is sombre and formal rather than approachable. The flat grey ground with no texture is also dim for the article pages, where visitors read long text.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose brief asks for a personal, approachable advisor. A visitor may take the solemn, monumental look as the institutional voice the brand sheet rules out.

findings.where: First screen and the whole tile
findings.fault: There is no photograph of Mark and no place set aside for one. The only picture is the enlarged mark. The direction gives the layout round nowhere to show 'the man himself', so a solo advisor's first screen has no face.
findings.who_objects: Agency staff checking whether a real, named person stands behind the advice. Mark, whose brief lists being seen as a client value.

findings.where: Motion sketch: the 'Lay again' control at the foot of the box
findings.fault: The box shows an easing curve and a table but never the element that enters. 'Lay again' seems to replay the hero mark, which is a full page or more above and out of view when the button is pressed. The press gives no result the visitor can see.
findings.who_objects: The founder or Mark reviewing the motion principle. They press 'Lay again', nothing visible happens, and they cannot judge the movement.

findings.fault: A button is styled as an underlined text link, borrowing the link's mark, while the page's other action is a filled red tablet.
findings.who_objects: A visitor, who expects an underlined word to go somewhere rather than replay an animation here.

findings.where: Type rules against the headings: the hero name, the article title, the 'Write to Mark' button and the nav
findings.fault: The type note says Cinzel words are always parted by interpuncts. The hero name uses them, even after the middle initial ('Mark · M · Moseley') and between 'Infrastructure · Advisor', which splits one phrase into two items. The article title and the button do not use them. The page breaks its own stated rule, and where the rule is applied it makes the name and role stutter.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor reading the headline, who meets an odd break in a plain phrase. Angélique, who cannot tell from the rule whether new post titles need interpuncts.

findings.where: Palette: the 'Lime' swatch ('AA' on a red block) beside 'Minium', and the 'Granite' swatch drawn as an empty outlined box
findings.fault: Lime is shown on a red block that matches the minium swatch next to it, so the palette appears to hold two reds. Granite is an empty outlined box that looks like a blank input field rather than a colour sample.
findings.who_objects: Mark and the next round's designer reading the tile, who can misread which colours the palette holds.

findings.where: Texture stand-in: the boxed 'STAND-IN' label inside the ashlar drawing
findings.fault: The label is set in tracked capitals inside its own outlined box, so it looks like a small outlined button.
findings.who_objects: A reviewer, who may try to click it.

findings.where: First screen: the line under the headline
findings.fault: The line says what Mark does, but not for whom (development banks and agencies) or in which regions he works. Within five seconds a visitor cannot tell the advice is aimed at them.
findings.who_objects: Development-bank staff, the stated audience, deciding in seconds whether this advisor fits their region and kind of project.
